Siege of Samaria
seej uv suh-MAIR-ee-uh
noun phrase (2 Kings 6-7)
From Samaria, the capital of the northern kingdom; chiefly the Syrian siege and miraculous deliverance recorded in 2 Kings 6-7, in the days of Elisha.

📖 Biblical Definition

The siege of Samaria most properly names the Syrian blockade of the northern capital in the days of Elisha, recorded in 2 Kings 6-7, when Ben-hadad's host shut up the city until a famine so terrible gripped it that an ass's head sold for fourscore pieces of silver and women boiled their own children. Into this extremity Elisha spoke the word of the LORD: on the morrow fine flour and barley should be sold cheap in the gate of Samaria. The king's officer scoffed, and the prophet told him he should see it with his eyes but not eat of it. That night the LORD made the Syrians hear the noise of a great host, and they fled in panic, leaving their tents, silver, and food; four lepers at the gate, going out in despair, discovered the empty camp and said, “This day is a day of good tidings, and we hold our peace.” The famine broke in a day, the cheap food was sold as Elisha had said, and the scoffing officer was trodden to death in the gate, seeing the plenty but not tasting it. The dictionary marks the siege of Samaria as a great display of the providence of God: He needs no army to rout an army, turning the tide by a sound in the night, vindicating His prophet's word, and feeding a starving city by the hand of four outcast lepers. It also reads the lesson of the lepers' conscience—that good news held selfishly is a sin—and the lesson of the scoffer, that unbelief shall behold the salvation of God yet have no part in it.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The Syrian siege of Samaria in Elisha's day, broken overnight when the LORD routed the host by a sound and four lepers found the empty camp (2 Kings 6-7); a display of providence vindicating the prophet's word, with the scoffer judged.

SIEGE OF SAMARIA, noun phrase. The Syrian blockade of Samaria in Elisha's day (2 Kings 6-7).

A famine so dire that an ass's head sold for fourscore pieces of silver (2 Kings 6:25).

Elisha foretold cheap food in the gate on the morrow (2 Kings 7:1).

The LORD routed the Syrians by a noise of chariots, and they fled (2 Kings 7:6).

Four lepers found the empty camp: “This day is a day of good tidings” (2 Kings 7:9).

📖 Key Scripture

2 Ki 6:25 — "And there was a great famine in Samaria: and, behold, they besieged it, until an ass's head was sold for fourscore pieces of silver, and the fourth part of a cab of dove's dung for five pieces of silver."

2 Ki 7:1 — "Then Elisha said, Hear ye the word of the LORD; Thus saith the LORD, To morrow about this time shall a measure of fine flour be sold for a shekel, and two measures of barley for a shekel, in the gate of Samaria."

2 Ki 7:6 — "For the Lord had made the host of the Syrians to hear a noise of chariots, and a noise of horses, even the noise of a great host: and they said one to another, Lo, the king of Israel hath hired against us the kings of the Hittites, and the kings of the Egyptians, to come upon us."

2 Ki 7:9 — "Then they said one to another, We do not well: this day is a day of good tidings, and we hold our peace: if we tarry till the morning light, some mischief will come upon us: now therefore come, that we may go and tell the king's household."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the danger is the naturalistic explaining-away of the deliverance and the loss of its lessons on providence, unbelief, and good news held selfishly.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the providence of God who saves without an army. Critical readers explain the Syrian flight as a chance rumour or a natural panic; the text ascribes it directly to the LORD, who “made the host of the Syrians to hear a noise of chariots.” The dictionary affirms the divine hand: God turned a hopeless siege in a single night, vindicated His prophet's precise word, and fed a starving city—needing neither sword nor numbers, but only a sound in the dark.

The account also preaches two abiding lessons the dictionary will not let slip. The four lepers, having found the abundance, rebuked themselves: “This day is a day of good tidings, and we hold our peace… we do not well.” Good news kept selfishly is a sin; the church that has found the bread of life is bound to carry the tidings to the starving. And the scoffing officer, who mocked the prophet's word, beheld the salvation of God with his eyes but, trodden in the gate, had no part in it—a sober figure of the unbeliever who sees the goodness of God yet tastes it not.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

From Samaria (Hebrew Shomron), the hilltop capital built by Omri; besieged by Ben-hadad of Syria in Elisha's day, and later by Assyria, which finally took it in 722 B.C.

expand to see more

Shomron, Hebrew, Samaria, the capital of the northern kingdom built by Omri.

Besieged by Ben-hadad king of Syria in the days of Elisha (2 Kings 6).

The famine measured by the ass's head and the cab of dove's dung.

The four lepers (Hebrew metsora'im) who found the abandoned Syrian camp.

Later besieged and taken by Assyria in 722 B.C., ending the northern kingdom.

Usage

"The pastor preached the siege of Samaria to display the God who routs an army by a sound in the night."

"He pressed the lepers' rebuke—good news held selfishly is sin—upon the silent church."

"She saw in the trodden scoffer the unbeliever who beholds God's salvation yet has no part in it."
